Trialing of Intrathecal Baclofen Therapy for
Refractory Stiff-Person Syndrome
J. Camp Newton, MD,* Michael E. Harned, MD,* Paul A. Sloan, MD,* and Sara S. Salles, DO Þ
Objective: Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare disorder of the cen-
tral nervous system characterized by stiffness and muscle spasms that
may be progressive in nature. When oral medication is inadequate to
control muscle spasticity, intrathecal baclofen may be used. W e report a
patient with severe SPS and glutamate decarboxylase negative
[GAD(j)] (note: GAD( j) indicates the patient has no antibodies to
GAD), refractory to oral standard therapies. The patient was effectively
trialed with an intrathecal catheter and subsequently treated with chronic
intrathecal baclofen, which provided significant relief of spasticity
symptoms.
Case Report: A 48-year-old white man with a history consistent with
SPS presented to the clinic. His previous history showed that he met
several diagnostic criteria for GAD( j) SPS and had a muscle biopsy
positive for myositis. Oral medications were unable to control his mus-
cle spasticity, preventing him from working. The patient received an
intrathecal trial using a lumbar approach for placement of a thoracic
catheter with an initial baclofen dose of 50 Kg/d. Gradual titration to
symptom relief was performed up to 150 Kg/d. Functional evaluation by
our physical therapist showed improved motor function, the temporary
catheter was removed, and a permanent intrathecal pump placed for in-
trathecal baclofen infusion. The patient reported excellent symptom re-
lief over the next 6 months and improved activity.
Conclusions: Refractory SPS is difficult to treat and has few thera-
peutic options. W e report a GAD( j) patient with SPS and resulting
debilitating spasticity that was refractory to oral medications who
underwent successful continuous intrathecal catheter trial of baclofen
over 4 days and subsequently went on to implantation of intrathecal
pump. The literature reports only 5 cases of GAD( j) SPS patients
treated with intrathecal baclofen therapy, and these resulted in poor
long-term success. Our patient completed a 4-day trial of intrathecal
baclofen titrated to effect before pump implantation. W e advocate con-
tinuous intrathecal trialing, as opposed to single-injection technique, to
possibly better determine the effective therapeutic dose and ensure
posttrialing successful therapy.
(Reg Anesth Pain Med 2013;38: 248Y250)
S
tiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare disorder (1 per 200,000)
of the central nervous system with autoimmune features
that usually presents in the fourth to sixth decade of life. Orig-
inally described in 1956 by Moersch and Woltman, it is char-
acterized by stiffness and paroxysmal spasms of the axial and
proximal extremity muscles that can be insidious or progressive
in onset.
1Y3 Spasms can occur spontaneously or be elicited by
external stimuli and may be violent enough to fracture bones.
These symptoms occur with the lack of other neurological
signs: weakness, sensory deficits, ataxia, cognitive impair-
ment, pyramidal tract signs, or lower motor signs. Diagnostic
criteria were originally established in 1989 by Lorish, but later
Grimaldi suggested that SPS could more simply be subdivided
into 3 main subgroups: (1) patients with associated organ-
specific autoimmune disease, (2) patients with neoplasms and
nonYorgan-specific antibodies, and (3) idiopathic, antibody
negative.

1Y3 Electromyography typically shows sustained motor
activity associated with SPS is identical to normal voluntary
motor activity.
1,3 The pathophysiology is related to disinhibition
of inhibitory motor neurons that leads to excessive activity of
agonist excitatory motor neurons. Normal motor function re-
quires coupling of excitatory (agonist) and inhibitory (antago-
nist) muscle groups. Loss of GABAergic ( F-aminobutyric acid
[GABA]) pathways is thought to result in tonic firing of motor
neurons at rest and excessive excitation in response to sensory
inputs.
4
Although the exact cause is unknown, there are several
variants, the most common being associated with antibodies
against glutamate decarboxylase [GAD(+)], an enzyme neces-
sary for the synthesis of GABA.
1Y3 The GAD status of a patient
is determined by testing for plasma antibodies present against
GAD. If GAD is inhibited by antibodies, reduced levels of
GABA result in decreased motor neuron inhibition and thus
continuous stimulation of muscles via excitatory motor neu-
rons.
5,6 However, it must be noted that antibodies to GAD alone
do not explain the complete syndrome of SPS. Indeed, our pa-
tient was GAD negative yet had the clinical picture and diag-
nosis of SPS. The mainstay for therapy for SPS patients has
been GABA agonists such as benzodiazepines and baclofen or
immunomodulation to reduce GAD antibodies.
5 Baclofen is a
direct agonist of GABA-B receptors and does not require en-
dogenous GABA to exert presynaptic inhibition at the brain and
spinal cord level. Intrathecal baclofen has been suggested for
patients with symptoms refractory to oral agents or associated
with intolerable adverse effects. Case reports utilizing intrathe-
cal baclofen for the treatment of SPS have included predomi-
nately GAD(+) patients
7 and only 5 case reports of GAD( j)
patients (ie, patients without antibodies to GAD) in the lit-
erature.
8Y10 It is unclear whether SPS patients who are GAD( j)
will respond to intrathecal baclofen in the same manner as GAD(+)
patients. Of the current 5 cases reported, only 2 patients went on
to chronic intrathecal baclofen pump. Of interest, a single injec-
tion intrathecal baclofen bolus was used to determine efficacy in
each of these cases, whereas the authors of this report have ad-
vocated for a continuous catheter trial over several days as a better
indication of successful outcome following intrathecal pump
implantation.
11
We report a patient with severe SPS and GAD( j), refrac-
tory to oral standard therapies, who was effectively trialed with

CASE REPORT
A 48-year-old man with a history consistent with SPS
presented to the clinic. His previous history showed that he met
several diagnostic criteria for GAD( j) SPS and had a muscle
biopsy positive for myositis. He had been a self-employed car-
penter until his muscle spasticity was no longer able to be
controlled with diazepam (10 mg 4 times a day) and baclofen
(20 mg orally 4 times a day), thereby preventing him from
working. Adverse effects of these oral drugs prevented upward
titration of the medications. He was able to walk without an
assist device but used a cane for long walks. He reported jaw
stiffness that interfered with mouth opening and was starting to
interfere with speech and the ability to eat. The patient received
disability benefits because of his stiffness and pain. Medical
history also included occasional blurred vision and shortness of
breath, hypertension, Prinzmetal angina, and deep vein throm-
bosis requiring anticoagulation.
On physical examination, the patient was walking with-
out an assistive device. He had jaw tightness, deep tendon re-
flexes 1/4 in upper and lower extremities, decreased light-touch
sensation in left upper and lower extremities, and decreased
range of motion in cervical/lumbar spine. His Ashworth scores
were 3 to 4 (Table 1) in the upper and lower extremities.
Before intrathecal catheter placement, the patient was
given appropriate education and evaluation, informed consent
was obtained, and he was instructed to hold warfarin for 7 days
before the procedure. On the morning of the trial, coagulation
results were confirmed to be normal, and informed consent was
reviewed. Antispasmotic medications were held the morning of
catheter placement, and precatheter assessment was performed
by the physical therapist, and documentation of the modified
Ashworth scale was recorded in proximal and distal muscle
groups of the upper and lower extremities. After receiving 2 mg
midazolam, intravenously administered, with local anesthesia
and using strict aseptic technique, a low lumbar paramedian
approach (17 g Tuohy epidural needle; intrathecal trial catheter,
Medtronic, Minneapolis, Minnesota) was used to place a tem-
porary intrathecal catheter. It was advanced to the T1 level under
fluoroscopy and documented with radiographs. The T1 catheter
tip level was chosen in an attempt to obtain relief of upper-
extremity and shoulder symptoms. The intrathecal catheter trial
was performed with an initial bolus of baclofen 50 Kg followed
by gradual increase of 50 Kg/d, up to a maximum 150 Kg/d,
where maximal effect was seen. Evaluation of motor tone by our
physical therapist was performed 2 and 4 hours after initiation of
trial, and the next day. Functional assessments along with any
drug adverse effects were recorded by the physical therapist
(Table 2). Maximal improvement in spasticity was reached
24 hours following initial baclofen trial. The intrathecal catheter
was removed, and the patient then discharged home.
During intrathecal baclofen trial, the patient showed im-
provements in modified Ashworth scores with a decrease of up
to 3 points in the upper extremities and 2 points in the lower
extremities (Table 2). The Ashworth scores were 1 in the
proximal extremities and 2 in the distal extremities at an intra-

thecal baclofen infusion rate of 200 Kg/d with no negative ad-
verse effects. Approximately 2 weeks later, the patient was
admitted and implanted with a permanent intrathecal drug de-
livery system (Medtronic SynchroMed II). The starting dose of
baclofen of 100 Kg/d and Ashworth scores of 3/4 distal and 1/2
proximal were re-recorded with no reported adverse effects. The
initial intrathecal baclofen dose following pump placement is
lower than the final baclofen trial dose because the patient has
just received sedation for pump placement and to avoid initial
complications such as bladder/urinary retention. The intrathecal

baclofen dose was increased the following day to 150 Kg/d with
Ashworth scores of 2 distal and 1 proximal recorded with no
reported adverse effects. Over the next 6 months, intrathecal
baclofen was titrated to muscle tone and symptom control with
a final intrathecal infusion rate of 200 Kg/d. At this dose rate,
the patient reported some residual spasticity (muscle tone at
clinic visit reported as 1+), especially in the masseter and neck
muscles (sternocleidomastoid). This neck spasm was treated
with botulinum A toxin injections and diazepam with overall
improvement in symptoms. After an additional 6 months of
therapy, the intrathecal baclofen dose had been gradually ti-
trated upward to 1050 Kg/d. This dose has changed little in
recent months (12Y18 months after pump implant) with a slight
upward dose titration to the current 1200 Kg/d. The patient has
reported no other significant adverse effects and with overall
satisfaction in his intrathecal baclofen therapy.
DISCUSSION
Refractory SPS is difficult to treat and has few therapeutic
options. Oral medications commonly used to treat spasticity,
such as benzodiazepines and baclofen, are limited by undesired
adverse effects and potentially life-threatening withdrawal ef-
fects (intentional or inadvertent) at higher therapeutic levels
required to treat SPS. Intrathecal baclofen is an effective therapy
for the management of spasticity commonly associated with
spinal cord injury and multiple sclerosis
12 and has been suc-
cessfully utilized in the management of SPS that is refractory to
oral therapy. Both high-dose oral baclofen and intrathecal bac-
lofen can have significant adverse effects following overdose or
acute withdrawal.
13 Intrathecal baclofen treatment should be
reserved for patients with symptoms refractory to oral therapy.
Baclofen’ s therapeutic efficacy is likely related to the activation
of presynaptic inhibition via GABA receptors in the spinal cord
and brain.
2,3 Baclofen activates GABA-B receptors present
on both presynaptic primary afferents and postsynaptic in-
terneurons.
4 It is possible that early in the disease GABAergic
neurons are still active, and as the disease progresses, the effects
of external ligands may wane, as is seen with our patient.
There are very limited studies with GAD( j) patients, and
long-term studies assessing the therapeutic effects of intrathecal
baclofen therapy on SPS are sparse. Future studies should
compare the effects of intrathecal baclofen in GAD( j)v s
GAD(+), and continued research is needed in evaluating the
long-term benefits of intrathecal baclofen in SPS. Although
complete remission was not obtained, our patient achieved
significant benefit in symptoms and quality of life (increased
physical activity, patient satisfaction) with intrathecal baclofen
implanted pump.
We report a GAD( j) patient with SPS and resulting de-
bilitating spasticity that was refractory to oral medications who
underwent a successful continuous intrathecal catheter trial of
baclofen over 4 days and subsequently went on to implantation
of intrathecal pump. Intrathecal baclofen has been utilized for
the treatment of refractory spasticity (eg, multiple sclerosis and
spinal cord injury) at doses of 12 to 1500 Kg/d with the majority
of patients being maintained at 300 to 800 Kg/d,
3,8,13,14 the end
point of baclofen therapy ideally being titration to therapeutic
effect or failure in efficacy due to undesirable adverse effects.

On follow-up in clinic at 6 months, the patient reported con-
tinued therapeutic benefit and minimal adverse effects with
increased activity and overall satisfaction at a dose of 460 Kg/d.
T ypical adverse effects are usually dose-related weakness and
sedation, but psychiatric disturbances, urinary frequency and
retention, constipation, vomiting, and hypersensitivity have also
been reported. The patient reported none of these adverse ef-
fects at 6-month follow-up, although he did receive botulinum
toxin A injections for stiffness in his neck and jaw.
The literature reports only 5 cases of GAD( j) SPS pa-
tients treated with intrathecal baclofen therapy, and these
resulted in poor long-term success. However, these trials uti-
lized a single-injection baclofen trial and did not undergo con-
tinuous intrathecal baclofen trialing before implantation. Our
patient completed a 4-day trial of intrathecal baclofen titrated to
effect before pump implantation. It is possible that continuous
intrathecal trialing, as opposed to single-injection technique,
allowed a better determination of the effective therapeutic dose
and ensure posttrialing successful therapy. Clearly, further re-
search needs to be done to determine exactly how intrathecal
trialing with baclofen should be accomplished in these patients
and whether trialing techniques will predict outcome of long-
term pump therapy.
